title: General Dynamics Corporation v. Superior Court (Rose)
lead: An in-house lawyer alleged retaliation for doing his job. California preserved the client’s power to end representation while allowing a contract claim and carefully confined routes to a public-policy tort.

actors.name: Andrew Rose
actors.role: Former General Dynamics employee and in-house lawyer

actors.name: Justice Arabian
actors.role: Author of the unanimous California Supreme Court opinion

proceedings: Trial court overruled a general demurrer; Court of Appeal denied General Dynamics’ mandate petition.
Supreme Court affirmed and remanded for proceedings including amendment of the tort allegations.
limits: The complaint’s allegations were accepted for a facial demurrer, not established as facts. No damages, reinstatement, or merits finding was awarded.
This is the 1994 decision; its professional-rule and privilege discussion is presented as the court’s historical analysis.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A promising career ends in disputed circumstances
sections.cue: Introduce Rose and distinguish his allegations from findings.
paragraphs: Andrew Rose alleged that he joined General Dynamics Corporation in 1978, aged twenty-seven, as a contract administrator at its Pomona plant. Commendations and promotions followed, and he said he was on course to become a division vice-president and general counsel. The company discharged him on June 24, 1991, citing loss of confidence.

Rose claimed that explanation concealed retaliation. He alleged that he had investigated workforce drug use, protested the failure to investigate bugging of the security chief’s office, and advised that a salary policy could violate the federal Fair Labor Standards Act and create substantial back-pay liability. Those were the complaint’s allegations, not findings about drugs, surveillance, compensation law, or the company’s actual motives.

Rose brought two theories. Assurances and the parties’ conduct allegedly created an implied agreement permitting discharge only for good cause. Separately, the alleged retaliatory reasons violated fundamental public policies. General Dynamics answered that an in-house lawyer could be discharged for any reason without either form of liability. The trial court overruled its general demurrer, and the Court of Appeal denied its petition for a writ of mandate. The California Supreme Court took up that categorical objection.

sections.title: Ending representation does not erase every promise
sections.cue: Explain why client autonomy did not defeat the contract theory.
paragraphs: General Dynamics relied on Fracasse, an earlier decision protecting a personal-injury client’s ability to dismiss contingent-fee counsel with or without cause. Fracasse limited counsel to the reasonable value of services, payable upon recovery. Justice Arabian’s unanimous Supreme Court opinion reaffirmed the client’s unilateral power to end representation, but explained that the power did not confer immunity from every monetary consequence. Fracasse addressed a particular fee arrangement and allocation of risk and itself recognized a compensation obligation. Permanent in-house employment involved different expectations and economic circumstances.

Rose sought damages, not an order compelling continued representation; reinstatement was unavailable. A client could remove an attorney it no longer trusted and still answer for prior contractual commitments. The court illustrated the distinction with a hypothetical lawyer who moved across the country in reliance on a fixed-term agreement. That example explained the rule; it was not Rose’s history.

Under Foley, California’s earlier employment-contract decision, Rose adequately alleged an implied good-cause agreement through career employment, promises of security and retirement benefits, favorable reviews, promotions, salary increases, commendations, and disregard of published discharge procedures. Matters of compensation, tenure and promotion could ordinarily be handled like those of other employees. Employers retained latitude to define good cause for confidential personnel. The court sustained the pleaded theory, without finding an actual agreement, lack of cause, or the absence of future privilege problems.

sections.title: Professional duties can support a limited remedy
paragraphs: The tort theory arose from public duties imposed by law, rather than the parties’ bargain. California required an established, fundamental policy benefiting the public, not simply an employee’s private interests. An in-house lawyer also owed dual obligations: loyalty to the client and compliance with mandatory professional norms. Economic dependence on one employer could make adherence costly and encourage silence.

The court examined Balla, Herbster and Willy, decisions denying lawyer-employees remedies because of confidentiality and existing duties to report or withdraw. It accepted the importance of confidences but rejected the proposition that ethical duties made a remedy redundant. Telling a lawyer to resign ignored the cost of compliance. Those duties could instead justify a confined remedy encouraging observance of public obligations. This reasoning did not eliminate confidentiality limits.

sections.title: Two paths require specific legal duties and protected proof
sections.cue: State the conditions Rose would have to meet.
paragraphs: The first question was whether discharge followed compliance with a mandatory ethical duty prescribed by professional rule or statute. The court gave refusal to commit a crime or professionally disqualifying misconduct as examples. If the lawyer’s conduct was merely permitted, rather than required, two further conditions applied: a nonlawyer must be able to bring a public-policy discharge claim for the same conduct, and an applicable statute or ethical rule must permit departure from confidentiality. General disagreement about desirable corporate policy would not suffice.

The relevant norm had to be unequivocal and protect the public at large. California’s governing rules and statutes supplied the ethical predicates; the American Bar Association’s model codes did not independently do so. For out-of-state conduct, the court suggested ordinary choice-of-law analysis. The lawyer bore the burden of identifying the norm and showing impermissible motivation under but-for causation. An employer could establish a legitimate alternative reason for discharge. These requirements made the lawyer’s tort remedy narrower than an ordinary employee’s.

Attorney-client privilege remained intact for in-house counsel. Existing statutory exceptions, including crime-fraud and specified prevention of criminal harm, remained available, but the tort created no blanket exception. A claim that could not be fully established without breaching privilege had to be dismissed. The court expected that issue usually to emerge in discovery or summary judgment, seldom, if ever, on a facial demurrer.

Sealing, protective orders, limits on admissibility and later use, and appropriate in-camera procedures could protect legitimate confidences while permitting proof. None authorized violating privilege. A lawyer who disclosed protected confidences in an unsuccessful action could face professional discipline.

sections.title: Rose receives an opportunity to amend, not a merits victory
paragraphs: Rose’s implied-contract allegations adequately pleaded the required elements. His tort allegations, however, did not identify the professional rule or statute requiring or supporting the conduct he said caused his dismissal. He apparently assumed that the ordinary employee’s tort rules applied without further restrictions.

Because no published California case had previously resolved this precise issue, the court allowed amendment to satisfy the standards it had explained. On July 18, 1994, it affirmed the Court of Appeal’s judgment and remanded through that court for further proceedings. Justice Arabian’s opinion was unanimous, joined by Chief Justice Lucas, Justices Mosk, Kennard, Baxter and George, and assigned Justice Turner. It expressed no opinion about the merits of any alleged retaliatory act and awarded neither damages nor reinstatement.
